output:
**What I found:** Your sign-in, compute and store came with the template, and nobody ever decided on them. The store no longer fits. Your backend already does by hand what a relational database does for you: uniqueness checks, retries on write conflicts, joins in application code, and readers for old document shapes. Switch to one relational database now, before the first customer (the record calls this MIGRATE). The deciding fact is that production holds no real customer data. Today the switch is a rewrite of the store layer plus a reseed. After customers arrive, every live row has to be moved in stages while old and new code run side by side.

**Why it matters:** If you stay, the one-in-eight commit tax and the workaround code keep growing, and every reporting feature (reports that join employers, employees, roles and assessments) adds another hand-built join. If you switch later, you take on a data migration with a rollback plan and dual running, at the same time you are serving your first customers. At tens of small customers, one relational node is well within capacity, so scale gives no reason to stay on a document store.

**Do this first:**
1. Count the store tax instead of relying on the estimate: `git log --format=%H --name-only | <script>` over the store-layer paths, giving commits touching the store divided by all commits. Save that number as the baseline.
2. Put a port in front of the new store so domain code never imports the vendor SDK. Run its contract tests against the real database, not a fake. Then delete the uniqueness checks, conflict retries, application-side joins and old-shape readers.
3. Before the first feature lands on the new store, run the walking skeleton: sign-in with one authorization check, deploy and rollback, a backup and restore drill, erasure of one data subject, a cross-tenant read that gets refused, and the hardest report.

**What I did not check:** This directory holds only the skill library, so I read no product code, infrastructure-as-code or git history. Every signal below comes from your description.
- The commit share. Run the step 1 count in the product repo.
- Whether sign-in and authorization rules are tied to the document-database vendor. Search for security-rules files and auth SDK imports.
- Workload shape and cost envelope, which decide the compute verdict. Write down which jobs run long, run in batches or run on a schedule, and the monthly cost ceiling at zero load and at your expected scale.
- Tenancy, residency and backup/restore targets. Those profile dimensions are blank and go back to `requirements-grounding`.

```text
Mode:            Review (tripwire fired; first real data pending)
Component:       Document database
Door:            ONE-WAY
Status:          INHERITED
Forcing need:    none found (choice never recorded)
Profile:         Domain shape: relational (employer, employee, role, assessment, report;
                 cross-entity uniqueness and joins). Access: reports joining all four.
                 Scale: tens of small tenants, single node. Isolation/residency,
                 lifecycle, cost: GAP
Evidence:        Reported, NOT VERIFIED: hand-written uniqueness checks, conflict
                 retries, app-side joins, old-shape readers; ~1 in 8 commits touch store
Verdict:         MIGRATE
Tripwires:       n/a for the old store; for the new one: store-touching commit share
                 above baseline + 50% at the quarterly review, owner = tech lead
Reversal cost:   Now: rewrite the store layer, reseed. Rises with every real customer
                 row (staged expand/contract, dual reads)
Handoff:         evolutionary-database-design (light: no live data, so fresh schema
                 + reseed rather than expand/contract)
Next action:     Count the store-commit baseline, then define the relational schema
                 behind an owned port
```
